text: Tissue repair after injury involves overlapping events: inflammation, re-epithelialization, neovascularization, and synthesis/stabilization of a fibrous extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeled over time. Transglutaminase (TG) family members are upregulated during wound healing and act as a novel class of wound-healing mediators, crosslinking proteins via ε(γ-glutamyl)lysine bridges. This stabilizes proteins and regulates the behavior of diverse cell types recruited to the damaged area. The article examines tissue transglutaminase (TG2), the most widely expressed TG family member, in wound repair. Drawing on early and recent literature, the authors show that multifunctional TG2 affects ECM stability and cell–ECM interactions, and consequently cell behavior across the different phases of wound healing, and highlight how TG2 itself might be exploited therapeutically.
